tech.name: Silicon-graphite composite anode for lithium-ion batteries
tech.summary: A porous silicon-graphite composite anode intended to increase lithium-ion battery capacity while limiting silicon expansion.
tech.intended_application: High-energy lithium-ion cells for portable electronics and electric mobility.

verdict.reasoning: The authors integrate the composite anode into laboratory coin cells and report quantitative cycling results with a graphite baseline. Repeat testing supports laboratory validation, but no relevant-environment or scaled assembly evidence is shown.

criteria.note: Silicon alloying and expansion mechanism are described.
The paper identifies high-energy cells as the application.
The composite anode architecture is specified.
A diffusion model supports the pore design.
Higher capacity and reduced expansion are expected benefits.
Measured capacity and cycling data are reported.
The work uses small laboratory cells.
Anode, electrolyte, separator and cathode are tested together.
Quantitative cycling is compared with graphite.
Three cells are tested, but uncertainty statistics are limited.

evidence.quote: Silicon stores lithium through alloying, but repeated expansion and contraction can disrupt the electrode structure.
evidence.why: The authors describe the scientific mechanism and its limitation.

evidence.quote: We formulate a porous silicon-graphite composite anode with a carbon binder network.
evidence.why: The specific material architecture is stated.

evidence.quote: Finite-element modelling predicted that the pore network would reduce local stress during cycling.
evidence.why: Modelling supports feasibility of the proposed structure.

evidence.quote: The composite anode was assembled in CR2032 coin cells and cycled against lithium metal.
evidence.why: The key electrochemical function is tested in a laboratory cell.

evidence.quote: The cells delivered an initial reversible capacity of 1,420 mAh/g at 0.1C.
evidence.why: A measured core-function metric is reported.

evidence.quote: After 200 cycles at 1C, capacity retention was 82%, compared with 61% for the graphite baseline.
evidence.why: Controlled cycling provides quantitative performance and a baseline.

evidence.quote: Three independently prepared cells showed similar capacity-fade profiles over 100 cycles.
evidence.why: Multiple cells provide limited repeatability evidence.

gaps.headline: The anode has not been tested in a scaled assembly under application-relevant conditions.

items.missing: Testing under elevated temperature, realistic current profiles and extended duration is absent.
items.why_it_matters: These conditions determine whether laboratory cycling translates to the intended application.

actions.step: Cycle pouch cells at application temperature and duty-cycle profiles.
actions.done_when: At least 10 cells retain 80% capacity after 500 equivalent full cycles.

items.missing: Only coin cells are reported; a scaled pouch-cell assembly is needed.
items.why_it_matters: Interfaces and heat transport can change at larger scale.

actions.step: Fabricate and test pouch cells using the composite anode and production-like interfaces.
actions.done_when: A pouch-cell batch completes formation and cycling with documented yield.

items.missing: Results are compared with a laboratory graphite baseline, not application specifications.
items.why_it_matters: Deployment decisions require evidence against customer and safety requirements.

actions.step: Define application targets for energy density, cycle life, safety and cost, then benchmark the pouch cells.
actions.done_when: A requirements matrix records measured values and pass or fail status.

risks: Silicon expansion may reduce pouch-cell cycle life.
Scale-up may introduce non-uniform current density.
Thermal management may differ from coin-cell tests.
assumptions: The intended application uses lithium-ion pouch cells.
The stated cycling protocol is representative of the target duty cycle.

next: Run realistic thermal and duty-cycle testing

summary.text: The paper demonstrates a porous silicon-graphite anode in laboratory coin cells. It reports high capacity, improved retention over graphite and limited repeat testing, supporting TRL 4. Evidence for TRL 5 is missing because the technology has not yet been tested in a scaled assembly under realistic application conditions.
key_takeaways: The composite anode has demonstrated its core function in laboratory coin cells.
Measured cycling results outperform the stated graphite baseline.
Pouch-cell and relevant-environment testing are the main next steps.
caveats: The example reports only three independently prepared cells.
No manufacturing yield or regulatory evidence is provided.

planned_items: Future work will evaluate pouch-cell assemblies.
